questions.q: According to this lesson, what follow-up question should come right after confirming a design "works"?
options: Is it the cheapest possible option?
Under what conditions does this stop working?
Who should get credit for this design?
Can this be deployed today?
questions.explain: Passing today's test is a low bar. Habitually asking under what future conditions (scale, change, an unstated assumption) the design would break catches far more real problems than stopping at "it works."

questions.q: What does "naming the trade-off out loud" mean as an architect habit?
options: Presenting the chosen design as having no downside at all
Explicitly stating what a design decision gives up in exchange for what it gains, rather than hiding the downside
Avoiding any discussion of alternatives entirely
Only discussing trade-offs privately, never with stakeholders
questions.explain: Every real architectural decision gives something up to get something else. Stating that trade-off explicitly (e.g., a batch job's delay in exchange for simpler error handling) respects the audience enough to let them weigh in, instead of asking for blind trust.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend finding your own design's weakest point before a design review, rather than waiting for someone else to find it?
options: Because it's considered rude to ever critique someone else's design
Because review boards never ask hard questions
Because bringing a known weak point into the room yourself builds trust and shows the design was actually stress-tested
Because it guarantees the design will be approved without changes
questions.explain: Naming your own design's weakest point before anyone else does signals genuine self-stress-testing, which builds far more trust with reviewers than presenting a design as flawless and getting caught by a weakness later.

questions.q: What distinguishes a real future requirement worth designing for, from a hypothetical one that leads to over-engineering?
options: Whether it would be fun to build
Whether the business has actually stated it as a known future requirement, versus merely being conceivable
Whether a competitor has already built something similar
Whether it adds the most technical complexity
questions.explain: A stated, known future requirement (e.g., the business has already said they're expanding to a second country next year) is worth designing for. A merely conceivable future ("they might someday...") is not — designing for it anyway adds cost and complexity without a real need behind it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say intellectual honesty about a design's weaknesses is a skill rather than a liability?
options: Because every real design has weak points, and architects who find them first earn more trust than those who get caught by them later
Because stakeholders prefer architects who never admit any flaw
Because it eliminates the need for a design review entirely
Because it is required by Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: Every real design has weak points. The only real choice is whether the architect surfaces them deliberately, ahead of time, or gets caught by them later — and reviewers consistently trust the former far more.
